## First LIVE occurrence outside a contention test — ops error sweep 2026-08-11/12

This ticket's mechanism (a write whose lock acquire times out is permanently lost) was observed **in a live external-integration run against real Jira DC**, not in a synthetic contention harness.

**Run:** GitHub Actions 'Live External Integration', 2026-08-10T06:31Z, run 31427-series (single failure in the sweep window 2026-08-05 -> 2026-08-12T03:30Z).

**Verbatim:**

    rebar._errors.RebarError: rebar create failed (exit 1): Error: git commit failed while holding lock: git timed out after 30s
    AssertionError: second pass: the repeated pass did NOT report convergence - it wrote something
    tests/external/live_jira_dc/test_reconcile_pass.py:184

**Why this is evidence for THIS ticket and not merely a slow-CI flake:** the two lines are causally linked in exactly the way this ticket predicts. The 30s lock-acquire timeout made pass 1's write disappear with no durable record; pass 2 therefore found the work undone and wrote it again, which broke the reconciler's **idempotency/convergence invariant**. The lost write is not just lost data here — it is observable as a correctness failure in a different subsystem, which is the strongest available argument that the terminal-and-lossy budget is not an acceptable steady state.

This also means the blast radius is wider than local high-concurrency use: a single ordinary CI runner under normal load can spend the 30s budget.

Related sighting the same week: tests/interfaces/store/test_git_contention_9305.py::test_concurrent_processes_through_seam_both_succeed failed 2026-08-11T13:05Z with 'writer beta failed' (assert 1 == 0 on the subprocess return code) - the same lock-contention family, from the regression test of bug 9305.

Reported by an automated ops error sweep; no code changed.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
## AC#1 RE-MEASUREMENT — post-R1/R3/R5 main, real-scale store (2026-08-11)

**Harness:** APFS clone of the live 737M tracker (~thousands of tickets), remote detached so
nothing escapes to origin. Writers are real `rebar comment` / `rebar claim` subprocesses.
Holder is a real second process taking the same dual-window lock via `lock.acquire()`.

### Result 1 — the original 6-writer harness NO LONGER loses writes. 7084 genuinely fixed it.

| concurrent writers | failures | writes lost | max elapsed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6  | 0/6  | 0 | 2.1s |
| 16 | 0/16 | 0 | 4.7s |
| 48 | 0/48 | 0 | 14.9s |

Short-write contention is now ~0.3s/writer and scales linearly. The 60s budget is not
reachable by writer count alone until roughly **200 concurrent writers**. The report's
headline measurement ("6/6 failures at exactly 60s, all six writes permanently lost") is
**no longer reproducible**. That half of the ticket should be rescoped.

### Result 2 — but the failure shape is UNCHANGED, and loss is still reachable. It is now driven by HOLDER DURATION, not writer count.

* **Holder 70s + 3 comments → 3/3 lost.** All exit 1 with
  `flock: could not acquire lock after 60s (holder: host=... pid=41052 held=77s pid_state=live)`,
  and `rebar show` afterwards contains **0 of the 3 markers**. Permanent, terminal loss,
  reproduced on current main.
* **Holder 45s + 1 `claim` → fails at exactly 30.30s**, `Error: could not acquire lock`.
  The claim is lost. This is the `attempts=1` budget on the most contended verb, and it is
  the FIRST thing to break under contention — it dies while comments alongside it survive.
* **The surviving margin is thin.** Holder 40s + 6 comments all succeeded, but at
  **59.5s of a 60s budget**. A holder a second or two longer would have lost all six.

### Root cause CONFIRMED (structural, not just empirical)

* `acquire()` computes `total_wait = timeout * attempts` and feeds **one** deadline shared by
  both legs (`_store/lock.py:695-698`). **`attempts` is not a retry loop** — it is a pure
  multiplier. Nothing anywhere re-attempts a timed-out acquire.
* Both legs **non-blocking poll with jitter** (50ms fcntl `lock.py:215`, 100ms mkdir
  `lock.py:628`). There is no FIFO and no fairness — waiters are a lottery, exactly as the
  report states.
* On timeout `LockTimeout` is raised and the write is discarded. The **only** retry in the
  codebase is `llm/completion_sidecar.py` (2 attempts, then drops the record with a bare
  `logger.warning`). Several call sites swallow it outright: `sync.py` reconverge `return`,
  `push.py` merge/commit, `ensures.py` warning-and-skip.

### Verdict

Premise **upheld, rescoped**. The write is genuinely terminal-and-lossy on current main —
AC#5's "test reproduces the loss" is satisfied above. What changed is the *trigger*: it is no
longer a 6-agent storm, it is any single holder that spends the budget (a reconciler pass, a
plan-review op, a slow CI runner — cf. the live Jira DC occurrence already recorded here).

**This evidence also selects the remedy.** Fair queueing / FIFO is the wrong fix for the
measured failure: when one holder exceeds the entire budget, *every* waiter fails regardless of
service order, so fairness buys nothing. The fix that matches the evidence is **bounded
retry-with-backoff** so a timed-out acquire re-attempts instead of discarding — loss becomes
latency — plus correcting `claim`'s 30s/`attempts=1`, which the measurement shows fails first.

Retry is safe here without phantom-write semantics: `LockTimeout` is raised by `acquire()`
**before** anything is staged or committed, so a re-attempt cannot double-write. That is what
makes this a mechanical fix rather than the R6 spool-and-adopt product decision that was
declined on 7084.

No code changed yet — this comment records AC#1 only.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
## Forensics: "the error surfaced but the write had LANDED", and the dead-holder wedge

Two field reports were raised against this ticket's design. Both were investigated read-only
against current `main`. Findings and their consequences for the retry design:

### 1. "Error reported but the write landed" — mechanism FOUND, and it does NOT threaten retry safety

A single `rebar transition <id> in_progress closed` takes up to **six** lock acquisitions, and
**five of them happen AFTER the STATUS event is durably committed** (`txn.py:299`, released at
`txn.py:311`):

| # | Site | On LockTimeout |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `txn.py:198` (write+commit) | exit 1, write did NOT land |
| 2 | `transition_close.py:433` completion signature -> `event_append.py:382` | **surfaces to the user** |
| 3 | `transition_close.py:454` `_apply_caused_by` | swallowed (`:255`) |
| 4 | `transition_close.py:472` force-close audit comment | swallowed (`:473`) |
| 5 | `transition_close.py:481` compact-on-close | swallowed twice (`:131` StringIO + `:133`) |
| 6 | `transition_close.py:490` push merge recovery | swallowed (`push.py:379`, `:735`) |

**The field report is #2.** The chain is `sign_completion_verdict` -> `signing.py:574 append_event`
-> `_seam.py:521 write_and_push` -> `event_append.py:382 write_lock` (60s) -> `LockTimeout` ->
`SigningError` -> `transition_close.py:440`, which prints:

    Warning: closed <id> WITHOUT a completion signature — flock: could not acquire lock after 60s (holder: ...)

**with exit code 0**, roughly 60s after the close already landed. That is exactly "reported a lock
error but had in fact landed". A second variant exists on the parent-first cascade
(`transition.py:399` / `claim.py:241`): the cascaded PARENT's transition commits and pushes, then
the child's acquisition times out and returns exit 1 — a different ticket's write landed.

**Consequence for this ticket's design: the safety argument survives, and is now evidence-backed.**
Each post-write step is an **independent event append with its own acquisition**. Retrying an
*acquisition* lands *that* event; it cannot replay the STATUS event, because the retry loop lives
strictly inside `acquire()` and is finished once `acquire()` returns. The double-append shape would
require retrying a layer ABOVE the lock, which this change explicitly does not do — and a
no-double-append test now asserts an appended-event count of exactly 1.

**Bonus:** `event_append.py:382` is one of this change's opt-in sites, so the completion-signature
append gains the retry ceiling. This change therefore *directly mitigates* the observed
closed-without-signature warning rather than merely coexisting with it.

The residual defect — that a best-effort post-write step reports a lock failure with **exit 0**
while silently downgrading the ticket to closed-without-signature — is a reporting/gate-integrity
problem in `transition_close.py`, outside this ticket's edit set. Filed separately.

### 2. Lock held ~12 min by an ALREADY-EXITED process — real bug, but a DISTINCT one

Two hypotheses were tested and **both refuted**:

* **Not an fd leak.** `os.open` fds are non-inheritable under PEP 446 (verified on this venv:
  `FD_CLOEXEC` set); there is **no `os.fork()`** anywhere in `src/rebar`; every lock-held spawn
  uses `close_fds=True`; `gc.autoDetach=false`/`maintenance.autoDetach=false` are set at
  `init.py:110-154`. A flock **cannot** outlive its process here.
* **Not `start=-` defeating the liveness proof.** On this macOS host the stamp is
  `host=name-... ns=- pid=... start=-`; host matches, both `ns` sides are `None` and compare equal,
  and a genuinely **dead** pid IS reclaimed at `lock.py:553-554`.

The actual hole is one step later, at **`lock.py:555-560`**. The recycled-pid discriminator is:

```python
if stamped_start is not None and current_start is not None and ...: return True   # inert on macOS
return False                                                                      # lock.py:560
```

On any platform without `/proc`, `_process_start_time()` **always** returns `None`, so line 557 is
**dead code by construction** and the function falls through to `return False`. When the original
holder is dead but its pid number has been **recycled** by an unrelated live process,
`_pid_alive()` says "live" and the lock is judged fresh. That branch is deliberately **exempt from
the 1h `_MKDIR_LOCK_STALE_CEILING_S` backstop** (`lock.py:516-519`, "never on a timer alone"),
because a live pid is treated as positive proof of liveness — which on macOS it is not. Net effect:
**an unbounded wedge**, matching the observed 12 minutes. Pid recycling is live on this host
(`kern.maxproc: 16000`; the counter has already wrapped past the observed stamp's pid).

A secondary, bounded (1h) wedge exists when `_reclaim_mkdir_lock` removes the owner file
(`lock.py:581`) but its `rmdir` fails (`lock.py:585`), leaving an owner-less dir that only the age
ceiling can clear (`lock.py:528-531`).

**Scope decision: NOT fixed here.** This lives entirely inside `_mkdir_lock_is_stale` /
`_reclaim_mkdir_lock` and shares no code with the retry seam. More importantly, changing when a
lock may be **broken** is a safety-critical behaviour change well beyond this ticket's approved
retry scope — getting it wrong breaks a live writer's lock. Filed separately as `discovered_from`.
Suggested direction recorded there: apply the age ceiling on the `lock.py:560` branch **only when
`current_start` is unavailable**, so "never break a live owner on a timer alone" still holds on
Linux while the no-`/proc` wedge becomes bounded.

comments.body:
## The gate lost its own PASS — this bug destroyed a 14-minute LLM review

While earning the plan-review attestation for THIS ticket, the bug this ticket describes
destroyed the review that was reviewing it. Recorded verbatim because it is the cleanest
in-the-wild instance yet, and it happened to rebar's own gate machinery rather than to a comment.

`rebar review-plan royal-weariless-zebrafish` completed with **`"verdict": "PASS"`, 0 blocking
findings, `"signable": true`** after ~14 minutes and 28 LLM calls. Neither the attestation nor
the review record survived:

    signature: {'signed': False,
                'error': 'flock: could not acquire lock after 60s
                          (holder: host=name-... pid=89059 held=103s pid_state=live)',
                'event': 'plan_review_generation_retry', 'retryable': True}

    plan review PASSED but the attestation could not be persisted:
      flock: could not acquire lock after 60s (holder: ... held=103s pid_state=live)
    run `rebar sign-review 10c3-5a33-2e25-4584` to re-sign from the recorded review (no LLM re-run)

The offered recovery **did not work**, because the PASS record itself was also lost:

    $ rebar sign-review 10c3-5a33-2e25-4584
    {"ok": false, "signed": false, "verdict": "BLOCK",
     "reason": "the latest review was not a signable PASS (verdict=BLOCK)
                — run `rebar review-plan` to produce a fresh verdict"}

So **two** writes were discarded by one contention episode: the signature AND the PASS sidecar.
The recorded verdict silently remained the PREVIOUS round's BLOCK, which is the worst shape — the
system does not merely lose the result, it retains a stale contradicting one. The full LLM review
had to be re-run from scratch.

### Why this is decisive evidence for the chosen remedy

* **The holder was `held=103s`, and 163s on a second sample** — far beyond the 60s budget. The
  re-measurement above established that writer COUNT no longer exhausts the budget; this shows
  holder DURATION routinely does, on an ordinary developer host with a handful of agents running.
  That is exactly the failure mode bounded retry addresses and fair queueing does not.
* **The retry ceiling would have saved it.** A 103s holder is inside the planned ~181.5s ceiling
  (3 passes x 60s + backoff), so the attestation write would have landed on pass 2 as latency
  instead of loss.
* **`event_append.py:382` is on the failing path** (`signing.py:574 append_event` ->
  `_seam.py:521 write_and_push` -> `event_append.py:382`) and is one of this change's three opt-in
  sites. This change therefore fixes this exact occurrence, not an analogue of it.

### Adjacent defect, NOT in this ticket's scope

`sign-review`'s advertised recovery path is only sound when the sidecar persisted but the signature
did not. When BOTH are lost to the same contention episode, the guidance printed to the user
("run `rebar sign-review` ... no LLM re-run") is misleading — it names a recovery that cannot
work, and the stale prior BLOCK is what `sign-review` then reports. Filed separately rather than
folded in here.

## Second consecutive PASS destroyed the same way — the gate cannot certify its own fix

Round 4 of `review-plan` on this ticket returned **`"verdict": "PASS"`, 0 blocking, 3 advisory,
`"signable": true`, `verified_at_sha: 54bdc0f8…`** — and was destroyed identically to round 3:

    plan review PASSED but the attestation could not be persisted:
      flock: could not acquire lock after 60s
      (holder: host=name-... pid=41427 held=88s pid_state=live)

`rebar sign-review 10c3-5a33-2e25-4584` again returned `verdict: BLOCK` (the stale prior round).
The response payload confirms **`"sidecar_emitted": false`** — so no PASS record was written at
all, and the advertised no-LLM recovery path has nothing to recover from. That corroborates the
adjacent defect noted in the previous comment: the printed guidance names a recovery that cannot
work when the contention episode takes the sidecar too.

**Running tally: two full plan-review PASSES (each ~14 min, 28 LLM calls) discarded by this
ticket's own bug, at holder durations of 103s, 163s and 88s.** All three exceed the 60s budget;
all three sit inside the planned ~181.5s retry ceiling, so the planned fix would have converted
every one of them into latency rather than loss.

Holder attribution: the long holders are other agents' `rebar transition` runs. That verb is the
heaviest writer in the system — `transition_close` alone takes up to six acquisitions (signature,
links, audit comment, compact-on-close, push). So the contention is not exotic; it is the fleet's
ordinary close path.

**This is a bootstrap deadlock worth recording as a first-class finding:** the plan-review claim
gate cannot certify a fix for the write-lock loss bug, because the write-lock loss bug destroys the
certification. The plan content is not in question — it has now PASSED twice with zero blocking
findings. Only the persist step fails. Escalated to the operator for a decision rather than
self-authorising the `--force` escape hatch.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
## Implemented — bounded retry inside `acquire()`

Claimed with a clean signed attestation (`verdict: certified`, head_sha `b13173bb7d`, 0 blocking).
The operator-approved `--force` fallback was **not** needed and was not used.

**`_store/lock.py`** — `acquire()` split into `_acquire_once()` (one pass against one deadline,
the previous body verbatim) plus a retry wrapper. New `retries: int = 0` on `acquire()` and
`write_lock()`; `write_path_retries()` reads `REBAR_LOCK_RETRIES` (default 2, clamped `[0,10]`,
malformed falls back rather than raising); `_retry_backoff_s()` is jittered
exponential-with-cap (0.5s, 1.0s, cap 2.0s) reusing `gitutil`'s `_jitter` / `_backoff_sleep`
seams rather than reimplementing them (plan-review A1 advisory).

**Opted in — exactly five sites, 3/1/1:** `event_append.py` (the three write-path
`write_lock()` calls), `txn.py` `_acquire_write_lock`, `push.py`'s locked commit-and-push.
Everything else keeps fail-fast through the `retries=0` default with no edit at all.

**`txn.py`** also stops swallowing the message: it now raises
`CommandError(f"Error: could not acquire lock — {exc}")`, so the cumulative wait and the holder
reach the caller instead of a bare generic string.

### Two decisions worth recording

**`retries=0` re-raises the ORIGINAL exception rather than rebuilding it.** Only the
retries>0 path constructs a new `LockTimeout` carrying measured cumulative elapsed. That keeps
the historical single-budget message byte-identical, which matters because
`test_lock_timeout_names_holder_7084.py:159` asserts **exact equality** on it and
`completion_sidecar.py:57` documents the string. A cumulative-elapsed message everywhere would
have broken both for no gain.

**The opted-in set is asserted by AST, not by line number.** `_opt_in_sites()` parses `src/` and
asserts `{"event_append.py": 3, "txn.py": 1, "push.py": 1}`. This plan was itself blocked once
for citing drifted line numbers (my base was behind `origin/main`), so a call-site inventory
keyed on line numbers would rot the moment anything above it moves. It also verifies the
negative half — that compaction, fsck, the doctor, the reconciler and the best-effort sweeps
did NOT gain retries — which a grep over changed files cannot.

### Verification

`tests/unit/test_lock_retry_zebrafish.py` — 20 tests, all passing. The RED/GREEN pair is
structural rather than temporal: the same subprocess holder outliving one budget loses the write
at `retries=0` and is ridden out at `retries=3`. Also covers no-double-append (the guarded body
runs exactly once under contention), loud exhaustion with cumulative wait + one warning per
exhausted pass, the claim shape, `txn` opt-in and message propagation, the `retries=0` default,
zero backoff when uncontended, and the env override incl. clamping.

`make lint` and `make typecheck` clean. `tests/integration/test_store_concurrency.py`,
`test_lock_timeout_names_holder_7084.py` and `test_store.py` pass unchanged (51 tests green).

`lock.py` is **797 lines** against the 800 cap — 3 lines of margin. Kept in place deliberately:
the retry cluster is well under the 100-LOC floor the module-size policy sets for a new file, so
extracting it would trade a real rule for a nominal one. Flagging it as the next edit's problem.

compiled_state.description:
## Context / Problem

A store write that cannot acquire the write lock in its budget is DISCARDED — no retry, no spool.
`acquire()` computes `total_wait = timeout * attempts` into **one** deadline
(`lock.py:695-698`), so `attempts` is a silent multiplier, not a retry loop. Both legs
non-blocking-poll with jitter (`lock.py:215`, `lock.py:628`), so there is no fairness.

Re-measured 2026-08-11 against an APFS clone of the live 737M tracker (numbers in the AC#1
comment): the 6-writer storm no longer loses writes (6/6, 16/16, 48/48 succeed — 7084's fixes were
real), but loss is still terminal and is now driven by HOLDER DURATION. A 70s holder + 3 comments
→ 3/3 exit 1 with **0 of 3 markers present afterwards**. A 45s holder + one `rebar claim` → fails
at exactly **30.30s** (`attempts=1`).

Confirmed since: the live Jira DC CI run recorded here, and TWO of this ticket's own plan-review
PASSES, destroyed by 60s timeouts behind 88-163s holders (see comments).


## Approach

**Bounded retry-with-backoff, not fair queueing.** When one holder outlives the whole budget every
waiter fails regardless of service order, so FIFO buys nothing here. Bounded re-attempts convert
loss into latency with less machinery than a queue.

Retry is safe without the phantom-write semantics that got R6 (spool-and-adopt) declined on 7084,
because **the retry lives strictly inside `acquire()`**: it re-attempts only the acquisition, and
`LockTimeout` is raised before the caller's write body runs. Once `acquire()` returns the loop is
finished and cannot re-enter, so no write is replayed. A retry ABOVE the lock would risk a
duplicate append; that boundary is asserted by test.

Checked against the "error surfaced but the write had landed" shape: one `transition` takes up to
six acquisitions, five AFTER the STATUS commit (signature `transition_close.py:433`, links, audit,
compaction, push). Each is an INDEPENDENT append with its own acquisition, so retrying an
acquisition lands *that* event and never replays the STATUS event. Opting `event_append.py` in also
makes the completion-signature append survive contention — the direct cause of the "closed WITHOUT
a completion signature" warning at `transition_close.py:440`.

1. `acquire()` and `write_lock()` gain **`retries: int = 0`**. The default of 0 reproduces today's
   behaviour exactly, so every caller not listed below is unchanged with no edit.
2. **Why passes rather than one longer budget:** both legs already poll to deadline, so a single
   180s budget would wait as long — but it would hold the won fcntl leg while starving on mkdir,
   and emit nothing until the very end. Discrete passes RELEASE between attempts, giving other
   waiters a window against the lottery-style polling, and give one warning per pass.
3. **Backoff schedule (pinned):** between passes the loop sleeps `_jitter(0.5 * 2**(n-1))` for
   pass *n*, capped at 2.0s — so ~0.5s then ~1.0s for the default 2 retries. Backoff is ADDITIVE
   to, not carved out of, each pass's `timeout*attempts` budget. Ceiling = 3 passes x 60s + ~1.5s
   backoff ≈ **181.5s**, the "~180s" figure below.
4. Opted-in sites pass `_write_path_retries()`, reading env **`REBAR_LOCK_RETRIES`** (int, default
   **2**, clamped `[0,10]`). `REBAR_LOCK_RETRIES=0` restores today's fail-fast.
5. The terminating `LockTimeout` names the **cumulative** wait plus the holder; each exhausted pass
   logs a warning naming it.
6. `txn._acquire_write_lock` (`txn.py:84-86`) discards both by re-raising a generic
   `CommandError("Error: could not acquire lock")`. It propagates `str(exc)` instead.

## Scope

**Edited, opting in to retries** (exactly five call sites):
- `src/rebar/_store/lock.py` — `retries` param, retry loop, backoff, `REBAR_LOCK_RETRIES` helper,
  cumulative-wait message, per-pass warning.
- `src/rebar/_store/event_append.py` — write path, `write_lock()` at **382, 420, 532**.
- `src/rebar/_commands/txn.py` — `_acquire_write_lock` (**84**) plus message propagation.
- `src/rebar/_store/push.py` — **654** (locked commit-and-push) opts in; **361** (advisory merge)
  stays fail-fast.
- `tests/unit/test_lock_retry_zebrafish.py` (new); `docs/concurrency.md`.

**Deliberately NOT edited — every other caller keeps fail-fast via the `retries=0` default:**
`compact_txn.py:340`, `compact_rebuild.py:126` (retries would undo 7084's R3 stand-aside and
re-create the 48s holder that caused this bug); `fsck_repair.py:241`, `s3_doctor.py:239`
(operator-driven repair); `inbound_translate.py:283`; `sync.py:255`, `push.py:361`,
`ensures.py:158` (best-effort sweeps).

## Testing

- **Happy path:** an uncontended `acquire(retries=2)` wins on pass 1 and never sleeps.
- **Reproduction (RED→GREEN):** a real subprocess holder held past one budget. With `retries=0` the
  waiter raises `LockTimeout` (today's loss); with `retries=2` it acquires on a later pass and its
  write is present.
- **No double-append:** after a contended acquire succeeding on a later pass, exactly ONE event is
  appended.
- **Exhaustion:** a holder outliving all passes raises `LockTimeout` with the cumulative wait, and
  one warning is logged per exhausted pass.
- **Claim path:** a claim-shaped acquire behind an over-budget holder succeeds on a later pass; its
  `CommandError` carries the cumulative wait and the holder.
- **Fail-fast preserved:** the advisory `push.py:361` merge acquires with `retries=0`.
- **Env override:** `REBAR_LOCK_RETRIES=0` restores fail-fast; out-of-range clamps.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] Re-measured post-R1/R3/R5 main and recorded whether writes are still lost — done, numbers in
      the AC#1 comment.
- [ ] The retry-vs-fair-queueing decision is recorded in Approach with its selecting evidence.
- [ ] A write whose first budget expires is re-attempted, verified by
      `pytest -q tests/unit/test_lock_retry_zebrafish.py -k reproduction` exiting 0.
- [ ] The retry never replays the write body, verified by the no-double-append test asserting an
      appended-event count of exactly 1.
- [ ] A write exhausting every pass raises `LockTimeout` naming the cumulative wait, verified by
      the exhaustion test's message assertion.
- [ ] `claim` succeeds on a later pass behind an over-budget holder, verified by the claim-path
      test.
- [ ] `claim`'s error text carries the cumulative wait, verified by asserting the `CommandError`
      message contains it.
- [ ] `claim`'s error text names the holder, verified by asserting the `CommandError` message
      contains the holder string.
- [ ] Opted-in sites are exactly five, distributed 3/1/1, verified by
      `diff <(grep -rln 'retries=_write_path_retries()' src/rebar --include='*.py' | xargs -n1 sh -c 'echo "$(basename $0) $(grep -c retries=_write_path_retries $0)"' | sort) <(printf 'event_append.py 3\npush.py 1\ntxn.py 1\n')`
- [ ] The advisory `push.py:361` merge stays fail-fast, verified by the fail-fast test asserting
      that acquire is called with `retries=0` on that path.
- [ ] Each exhausted pass logs a warning naming the holder, verified by a caplog test asserting one
      record per exhausted pass.
- [ ] The `retries` default is 0 so unedited callers are unchanged, verified by a test asserting
      `inspect.signature(lock.acquire).parameters['retries'].default == 0`.
- [ ] `REBAR_LOCK_RETRIES=0` restores fail-fast, verified by the env-override test.
- [ ] Out-of-range `REBAR_LOCK_RETRIES` clamps to `[0,10]`, verified by the clamp test.
- [ ] `docs/concurrency.md` documents the ~180s ceiling, verified by
      `test "$(grep -c '180' docs/concurrency.md)" -ge 1`.
- [ ] `docs/concurrency.md` documents the override, verified by
      `test "$(grep -c REBAR_LOCK_RETRIES docs/concurrency.md)" -ge 1`.
- [ ] `make lint` exits 0.
